newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's Bruton sees new IRA truce inevitable.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Bruton sees new IRA truce inevitable.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Wednesday he believed a new IRA ceasefire was inevitable eventually because the principle demand of Irish republicans was for entry to peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland.
But he told parliament he could not say if the Irish Republican Army (IRA) would call a new truce in the short term.

Sinn Fein, political wing of the IRA, has been barred from current multi-party peace talks because the guerrillas have failed to renew the truce in their 25-year war against British rule in Northern Ireland.
The IRA broke a 17-month ceasefire last February with a bomb in London which killed two people. It has since set off a series of bombs on the British mainland.
Bruton said on a recent trip to Washington he was hopeful the ceasefire would be restored, sparking speculation that a new truce was imminent. Republican sources strongly denied this.
Bruton said there was an opportunity for Sinn Fein to play its part in the shaping of a new political settlement through the peace talks.
"That makes the restoration of the IRA ceasefire a matter of such compelling logic that its inevitability can scarcely be in doubt," he said.
"It would be so much better for everybody, including the republican movement, if they acted on that logic now or in the very short term. Whether this will happen, I cannot say."

Bruton also said the discovery of arms and explosives by British police during raids in London on Monday undermined the position of those advocating a peace strategy and diminished hopes of a ceasefire.
"It does not inspire confidence that the Sinn Fein leadership is successfully persuading republicans to move in a peaceful direction," Bruton told parliament as it resumed after a summer recess.

Asked about the death of Diarmuid O'Neill, an IRA suspect shot dead in Monday's police action, Bruton said responsibility for his death lay with those who had failed to call an IRA ceasefire and who had put him "into the sort of work he was doing."
Five other people were arrested and 10 tonnes of explosives seized in the raids.
